title: Sludge Digestion for Wastewater Operators
audience: Operators, trainees and supervisors who run or support the solids handling at a municipal wastewater plant and want a clear foundation in sludge stabilisation and digestion, ideally after a thickening course.
prerequisites: Basic arithmetic. Basic Math and a thickening course are helpful but not required. Jurisdiction-neutral: no regulatory limits are stated in this course.
introduction: Learn why wastewater sludge is stabilised and how the arithmetic of volatile solids and volatile solids reduction works. Then follow anaerobic digestion, with its stages, temperature, mixing, feeding, retention time, volatile acids and alkalinity, gas and the signs of a sour digester, and aerobic digestion with the additional methods of lime stabilisation and composting. Finish with monitoring, sampling, records, digester loading and the way thickener output reaches the digester. Each module has a worked scenario, quick checks that explain the reasoning behind each answer, and a short written assignment. The course gives general principles and recognition-level safety content only. Plant-specific limits, procedures and safety permits come from your own plant and regulator.
delivery: Self-paced lessons, optional quick checks, a graded final exam and a non-credit certificate. Duration is being validated; no contact-hour award is made.

modules.title: Why stabilise sludge: volatile solids, pathogens and odour
objectives: Explain why sludge is stabilised and how volatile solids, pathogens, odour and vector attraction are linked to it.
Use the volatile solids reduction formula and the mass of volatile solids to read a simple digestion mass balance, and compare aerobic and anaerobic digestion at overview level.
modules.lesson: ### What stabilisation means Thickened sludge may still need stabilising. It holds organic matter that can rot, organisms from the wastewater that can cause disease, and the potential to smell and to draw flies. Stabilisation is the group of treatment steps that makes the solids safer and less offensive to handle, store, haul and reuse. The Wisconsin study guide gives the purpose of sludge treatment as reducing organic content and pathogenic organisms so that the material can be reused while public health and the environment are protected. It describes treated, or stable, sludge as having less odour, which reduces vector attraction, and more public acceptance. The guide also lists good dewatering properties, although dewatering depends on the process. The WEF manual says the same thing in other words: stabilisation processes further treat the sludge to reduce odours or nuisances, to reduce pathogens, and to make disposal or reuse efficient. ### Volatile solids and fixed solids Sludge solids are not all alike. Part of the solids is organic. It came from living cells and food waste, and microbes can eat it. Laboratories report this part as volatile solids. The rest is the fixed solids, the inorganic material such as grit that stays behind as ash when the organic part is burned off. In the Wisconsin guide's words, the volatile (organic) solids in the feed are used as food by the bacteria in a digester. That is why volatile solids are the quantity that digestion works on. Total solids tell the plant how much dry material it has. Volatile solids are a laboratory estimate of the organic part, and only some of it can still rot. ### Pathogens Wastewater solids can carry disease-causing organisms, so one aim of stabilisation is to lower their numbers. Different processes do it in different ways. Heat does it in thermophilic digestion and in composting. High pH does it in lime stabilisation. A long, active biological process does it in an aerobic digester. The WEF manual notes that some regulators group the result into classes. The US federal rule it describes has two levels, Class A and Class B, and Class A is the more stringent. This course states no criteria. Your own regulator and permit say which ones apply to your plant. ### Odour and putrescibility Putrescible means able to rot. Sludge that still holds a lot of easily digested volatile solids will keep rotting in a tank, a truck or a storage pile, and the rotting is what produces the smell. Aerobic digestion is described in the WEF manual as making the digested sludge less likely to generate odours during disposal. The same manual warns that composting under anaerobic conditions can produce significant foul odours, which is why composting tries to keep the pile aerobic. ### Vector attraction In this course, a vector is an animal, such as a fly or a rodent, that can carry disease from the solids to people. The WEF manual says vector attraction reduction requirements are meant to reduce putrescibility, because highly putrescible solids tend to attract flies and rodents. Stabilised solids are less appealing to them. Regulators accept several ways of showing this. One is a measured reduction in volatile solids. For aerobically digested sludge, another is an oxygen uptake test, which shows how actively the microbes in the sludge are still using oxygen. Again, your regulator sets the test and the result that count. ### Two biological ways to stabilise Both common digestion processes use microbes to destroy volatile solids. In aerobic digestion, long-term aeration supplies oxygen and the microbes use up the organic matter. In anaerobic digestion, the tank is sealed to keep oxygen out, and a different set of microbes breaks the solids down and makes methane gas, which can be recovered and used as an energy source. The Wisconsin guide names these two as the most common treatment processes. It lists composting, lime stabilisation, pasteurisation and heat drying as other processes. Modules 2 and 3 take each in turn. ### Anaerobic and aerobic digestion compared Most municipal digesters of the anaerobic type are high-rate systems that are mixed and heated. They make fuel gas, but the gas is a hazard and the methane-forming microbes are easily upset. The WEF manual describes aerobic digestion as simple to operate, low in equipment cost, and free of explosive digester gas. Its disadvantages are high energy cost for aeration, less biological heat in cold weather, loss of alkalinity, and in the past poor pathogen and volatile solids reduction. The manual says aerobic digestion has been used primarily at smaller plants, although in recent years it has also been used at larger ones. The WEF manual adds that aerobic digestion was first used where the sludge was waste activated or trickling filter sludge with no primary settling, and that anaerobic digestion was the usual choice when primary sludge was part of the feed. Neither process is better in every case. The choice depends on the plant, and your plant manual governs how you run yours. ### Where stabilisation fits in the solids train The WEF manual lists the solids treatment steps as thickening, dewatering, stabilisation and disposal, and says together they represent a major portion of the cost of wastewater treatment. Thickening normally comes first, and its output sets the volume that stabilisation has to handle. Stabilisation changes what the solids are. Dewatering and disposal usually follow. A change at one step passes to the next, which is why the last module returns to the way thickener output affects a digester. ### Volatile solids reduction Volatile solids reduction, or VSR, is the share of the volatile solids fed to a digester that has been destroyed. The WEF manual gives it as VSR in percent equals the volatile solids fed minus the volatile solids in the digested sludge, divided by the volatile solids fed, times 100. It states that anaerobic digestion typically reduces the mass of volatile solids by 40 to 60 percent. That is a typical range quoted for design, not a target for your digester. ### A worked VSR example A digester receives 4,200 pounds of volatile solids per day. The digested sludge leaves carrying 2,310 pounds per day of volatile solids. The volatile solids destroyed are 4,200 minus 2,310, which is 1,890 pounds per day. The VSR is 1,890 divided by 4,200, times 100, which is 45 percent. ### Finding the volatile solids in a volume of sludge The pounds of volatile solids in a volume of sludge are the gallons, times 8.34 pounds per gallon, times the specific gravity, times the solids as a decimal, times the volatile fraction as a decimal. For 10,000 gallons of sludge at 3.0 percent solids, of which 70 percent is volatile, with a specific gravity of 1.00, the answer is 10,000 times 8.34 times 1.00 times 0.03 times 0.70, which is about 1,751 pounds of volatile solids. ### Reading a laboratory report A digester feed report usually gives total solids as a percent of the sludge and volatile solids as a percent of the total solids. For example, a sludge at 4.0 percent total solids with 75 percent of those solids volatile holds 3.0 percent of its weight as volatile solids. The fixed (ash) share is the matching arithmetic: 100 percent minus the volatile percent, so a 75 percent volatile sludge is 25 percent fixed. Check which base the laboratory used before you multiply. A volatile figure quoted as a percent of the sludge and one quoted as a percent of the total solids differ by a large factor, and mixing them up gives a loading that is wrong by the same factor. ### Use masses, not just concentrations Digestion destroys volatile solids, so fewer volatile solids leave a digester than enter. Concentration also depends on the water in the sludge. A drop in percent volatile solids from feed to digested sludge is not the VSR, because the flows and total solids may differ. The WEF manual describes the approximate mass balance method, which multiplies each flow by its volatile solids concentration. It assumes the daily flows are steady and uniform in composition. When you compare feed and digested sludge, convert both to pounds per day first. The manual also describes the Van Kleeck method, which works from the volatile fractions of the feed and digested sludge and suits digesters without significant grit build-up. Using one method the same way each time keeps trends comparable. ### What VSR does and does not tell you VSR depends on the sludge as well as on the digester. The WEF manual notes that waste activated sludge from a system with a long solids retention time holds a low fraction of biodegradable material, so it has less to lose. A low VSR can therefore come from a stable feed as well as from a poor digester. Use it as a trend for your own plant, and compare it with gas production, temperature and the other measurements in the next modules. ### Checking the arithmetic A VSR cannot exceed 100 percent, and the volatile solids leaving a digester should not exceed those entering unless something has been added, the tank's stored solids are being drawn down, or the samples were taken at different times. If a calculation gives an odd result, recheck the units and whether percent has been written as a decimal. Write every answer with its unit, because pounds, pounds per day and percent are easy to mix up on a log sheet.

checks.prompt: What is the main purpose of stabilising sludge?
choices: Cut pathogens and the tendency to rot so odour and vector attraction fall
Remove free water so the same solids sit in a smaller volume
Raise the fixed solids share so the sludge settles more quickly
Concentrate the solids so the digester receives a thicker, steadier feed
checks.explanation: Stabilisation lowers the tendency to rot and pathogen levels so odour and vector attraction fall, whereas removing water or concentrating the feed is thickening or dewatering, and a higher fixed share does not make sludge stable.

checks.prompt: Which description fits volatile solids?
choices: The inorganic part of the solids that remains after burning a sample
The organic part of the solids, part of which microbes can use as food
The part of the solids that dissolves and passes through a filter
The water that evaporates when a sludge sample is dried
checks.explanation: Volatile solids are a laboratory estimate of the organic fraction, part of which microbes use as food, not the inorganic ash left after burning, not a fraction defined by what passes a filter, and not evaporated water.

checks.prompt: What does vector attraction reduction aim to do?
choices: Dry the solids so quickly that insects stay away from the pile
Add chemicals that mark the pathogens for later laboratory counts
Make the solids less likely to attract flies and rodents
Lower the volume of sludge so fewer trucks visit the site
checks.explanation: Vector attraction reduction makes solids less likely to attract flies and rodents, mainly by reducing putrescibility; drying fast does not by itself change putrescibility, and neither do tagging pathogens or cutting truck trips.

checks.prompt: A digester is fed 6,000 lb of volatile solids per day and the digested sludge carries 3,300 lb per day. Using VSR percent = (VS in minus VS out) divided by VS in, times 100, what is the VSR?
choices: 55 percent
18 percent
82 percent
45 percent
checks.explanation: VSR = (6,000 - 3,300) / 6,000 x 100 = 45 percent; 55 percent is the share left, not the share destroyed; 18 and 82 percent do not come from these two loads.

checks.prompt: Which is a recognised advantage of anaerobic digestion?
choices: It makes methane gas that can be used as an energy source
It needs no heating or mixing, so its energy use is very low
Its operation is simpler than aerobic digestion, with fewer hazards
It avoids the need for gas detectors around the tank
checks.explanation: Anaerobic digestion makes methane that can fuel boilers and engines, while the other options wrongly claim no heat or mixing, simpler operation than aerobic digestion, or no need for gas detectors.

checks.prompt: A digester is fed 9,000 gal per day of sludge at 4.0 percent solids, 70 percent of which is volatile. Use a specific gravity of 1.00 and 8.34 lb per gal. How many pounds of volatile solids are fed per day?

21,017 lb per day

modules.title: Anaerobic digestion: stages, control and gas
objectives: Describe the stages of anaerobic digestion and how temperature, mixing, feeding and retention time keep the methane formers healthy.
Use the volatile acids to alkalinity ratio, retention time and gas production to judge digester health, and recognise a sour digester and the main digester gas hazards.
modules.lesson: ### The digester as a sealed biological reactor An anaerobic digester is a sealed tank in which microbes that do not use oxygen break down the volatile solids in sludge. The WEF manual calls it a multistage biochemical process that can stabilise many kinds of organic material. The tank is sealed because the microbes that make methane are anaerobic, so oxygen has to be kept out. Most municipal digesters are conventional mesophilic units in which all the stages happen in one vessel. The high-rate version is mixed and heated, and the manual says its uniform conditions give shorter detention time and more stable operation than the old unmixed design. ### The stages of digestion The WEF manual describes three basic stages. In the first, enzymes working outside the cells break solid compounds such as cellulose, proteins and lipids into smaller soluble compounds such as sugars, amino acids and fatty acids. Later steps make the other products. In the second, acid formers turn those products into acetic acid, propionic acid, hydrogen, carbon dioxide and other organic acids. In the third, two groups of methane-forming microbes work. One group converts hydrogen and carbon dioxide to methane. The other converts acetate to methane and bicarbonate. The Wisconsin guide gives a shorter version of the same story: enzymes break down solids, acid formers make volatile acids, and methane formers turn the acids into methane and carbon dioxide. ### Why the methane formers set the pace In most cases the methane formers control the process. The WEF manual says they are very sensitive to environmental factors such as high ammonia, low phosphorus, low pH, temperature and toxic substances, and that they reproduce very slowly. The acid formers work much more quickly. The Wisconsin guide states the consequence: if the acid former population grows too rapidly and makes excess volatile acids, a digester upset follows. Good operation therefore means keeping conditions favourable for the methane formers and not shocking them. ### Temperature The WEF manual gives the mesophilic range as 32 to 38 degrees C (90 to 100 degrees F) and says digestion nearly stops at about 10 degrees C. Thermophilic digestion runs at 55 degrees C or higher, mainly to get greater pathogen destruction, and it needs much more heating energy. Whatever temperature is chosen, it should be held steady. The manual describes temperature stress as a change of more than 1 or 2 degrees C in under 10 days, which slows the methane formers while the acid formers carry on making acid. The Wisconsin guide gives a daily figure, saying a change of more than 1 degree F per day affects the methane formers, and the WEF manual advises logging the temperature daily so that swings are caught. Below the mesophilic range the process slows, and above it the manual says efficiency does not improve and energy is wasted. ### Primary and secondary digesters Medium and large plants usually have both. The Wisconsin guide says primary digesters are mixed and heated and do most of the stabilisation, gas production and pathogen reduction. Secondary digesters often serve as storage for digested sludge, a standby primary tank, a source of seed sludge and a quiet basin where supernatant can be drawn off. The WEF manual says decanting means stopping the mixing so the contents can settle, so it is not recommended for primary digesters. A tank in service as the primary is kept mixed and heated so that the sensitive methane formers can work steadily. ### Mixing Mixing together with heating, uniform feed and thickened feed provides good conditions for the microbes. The WEF manual lists its benefits: it spreads the incoming solids through the tank and gives them contact with the microbes, prevents thermal stratification, reduces scum and the build-up of settled material, dilutes inhibitors such as toxic material or feed at the wrong pH or temperature, and helps gas separate from the liquid. Unmixed digesters stratify, with scum on top and stabilised solids and grit on the floor. Grit that is allowed to settle takes up active volume. If a mixing pump shows a large pressure rise at the discharge, the manual says that may indicate clogged piping or nozzles. ### Feeding Uniformity is the key. The WEF manual says sudden changes in feed volume or concentration, temperature, composition or withdrawal rate inhibit digester performance and may lead to foaming. The ideal is continuous feeding of a blend of primary and waste activated sludge. Where that is impossible, a short feed cycle every hour is used, and a small plant on a single shift feeds at least three times. The Wisconsin guide gives the reasons for feeding thick sludge in small amounts, often: lower heating cost, less supernatant, fewer upsets, longer detention time and steadier gas production. Solids are withdrawn at least daily, so the microbe population and the buffering balance do not drop suddenly. ### Retention time and loading Solids retention time, SRT, is the mass of solids in the digester divided by the mass of solids removed each day. Hydraulic retention time, HRT, is the digester volume divided by the liquid removed each day, including any decant. Without decanting, and in a well-mixed digester, the two are the same. The WEF manual says high-rate digesters are typically sized for an SRT of 15 to 20 days. With total detention times much shorter than 15 days, the methane formers cannot reproduce quickly enough to replace those that leave, and the buffering capacity falls. Pumping dilute sludge shortens detention time. The manual gives a typical organic loading rate for a mixed, heated digester as 0.1 to 0.2 pounds of volatile solids per day per cubic foot. These are typical figures from the manual, not limits for your plant. ### Volatile acids, alkalinity and pH Volatile acids are intermediate by-products of digestion. Alkalinity is the buffering capacity that resists changes in pH. The ratio of volatile acids to alkalinity, written VA:Alk, is the volatile acids concentration divided by the alkalinity concentration, both in mg/L as CaCO3. The WEF manual calls it an excellent indicator of digester health. It gives approximately 0.1 to 0.2 as the normal ratio, treats a ratio above about 0.3 to 0.4 as an upset needing corrective action, and says pH depression and inhibited methane production occur above 0.8. The desired pH range is 6.8 to 7.2. The pH is a late warning. During an upset, volatile acids can rise while alkalinity still holds the pH, and the pH can fall noticeably as that buffering wears out, by which time the digester may be failing. ### Gas production Methane forms in the last stage, and carbon dioxide also forms earlier. The WEF manual says gas production is directly related to the volatile solids destroyed, with typical values of 12 to 18 cubic feet per pound destroyed, and that it is used as a measure of overall performance. The gas is mostly methane, about 60 to 65 percent, with 35 to 40 percent carbon dioxide. If gas production per pound of volatile solids destroyed starts to fall, the biology may be upset, and gas leaks and meter problems should also be checked. Plants log gas production against measured volatile solids destruction so that they can see this early. Scum is a related surface build-up: it is undigested grease and oil with buoyant material such as plastics, and good mixing blends it back into the tank. ### Using the gas Digester gas can fuel the boilers that heat the digesters. It can also drive engines and turbines for pumps, blowers or electricity, and heat recovered from engines can heat the digesters. A waste gas flare disposes of surplus gas, and untreated gas should not be released freely. The WEF manual says the gas may need treatment before use. Moisture, hydrogen sulfide and siloxanes damage pipes, valves, engines and boilers, and the more demanding the equipment, the cleaner the gas has to be. ### Digester gas safety Digester gas is flammable when mixed with air, and its main components are colourless, odourless and can displace air, which can cause asphyxiation. Hydrogen sulfide is also toxic, and the WEF manual warns that after a short exposure the nose goes numb to its odour, so the smell is not a reliable warning. Gas-handling systems are kept under positive pressure to keep air out, and drawing a digester down too far can pull air in. The pipework carries flame traps to stop a flashback, but gas expanding in the pipe can rupture it before the trap acts, which is why the trap sits close to the point of combustion. Pressure and vacuum relief valves protect the cover from over-pressure and from collapse. Detectors, nonsparking tools, ventilation, and regular inspection of the safety devices are part of the picture. A digester that has been emptied, and the space under a digester cover, count as confined spaces. This course covers recognition only. Written procedures and your safety training govern any work around the gas or inside these spaces. ### Digester upsets and the sour digester The WEF manual gives four basic causes of upsets: hydraulic overload, organic overload, temperature stress and toxic overload. The Wisconsin guide describes a sour digester as one that is not performing well, with low gas production, a high VA:Alk ratio and often a low pH, most often caused by excess organic loading. The WEF control strategy has four steps: stop or reduce the solids feed, find the cause, correct it, and provide pH control until the process recovers. The Wisconsin guide lists the key factors for optimal operation as organic loading, the VA:Alk ratio, temperature, mixing, SRT, pH, grit and scum, and toxicity. The WEF monitoring table also includes the carbon dioxide share of the gas as a daily check. Organic overload is also the most common cause of foaming, because acid formers outrun the methane formers and release carbon dioxide. Feeding continuously and blending the sludges well before feeding reduce that risk.

checks.prompt: Which order describes the stages of anaerobic digestion?
choices: Methane formers make methane, then acid formers make acids, then solids break down
Ammonia is nitrified, then denitrified, then the solids settle out
Solids break down, acid formers make acids, methane formers make methane
Acid formers make acids, then solids break down, then the tank is vented
checks.explanation: Solids break down first, then acid formers make volatile acids, then methane formers make methane; the other orders reverse the stages or describe nitrogen transformations, which are not anaerobic stages.

checks.prompt: Which group of microorganisms usually controls the digestion process?
choices: Acid formers, which are the most sensitive group in the tank
Nitrifiers, which keep the alkalinity high in the tank
Filamentous bacteria, which keep the sludge settling well
Methane formers, which grow slowly and are easily inhibited
checks.explanation: Methane formers control the process because they grow slowly and are easily inhibited, whereas acid formers are the less sensitive group and nitrifiers or filaments are not the controlling group.

checks.prompt: An anaerobic digester holds 800,000 gal and receives 40,000 gal of sludge per day. No decanting is used, the same 40,000 gal per day is removed, and SRT equals HRT. Using HRT in days = volume divided by daily volume removed, what is the HRT?
choices: 20 days
50 days
0.05 days
32 days
checks.explanation: HRT = 800,000 / 40,000 = 20 days; 50 days and 0.05 days come from inverting the division (0.05 is a rate per day), and 32 days comes from adding instead of dividing.

checks.prompt: A digester sample shows volatile acids of 600 mg/L and alkalinity of 2,400 mg/L. What is the VA:Alk ratio?
checks.explanation: VA:Alk = 600 / 2,400 = 0.25; 4.00 inverts the ratio and 0.75 and 0.025 are slips in the division.

checks.prompt: Why is pH a late warning of a digester upset?
choices: The pH probe responds slowly because gas bubbles cover its surface
Acid formers keep the pH steady until the methane formers have died
Acids can build while alkalinity holds the pH, which falls later
Alkalinity rises during an upset and holds the pH up for several weeks
checks.explanation: Volatile acids can rise while alkalinity holds the pH, so pH falls later as the buffer weakens. The other options name a probe fault, acid formers steadying pH or alkalinity rising, none of which is the reason.

checks.prompt: Which statement about digester gas safety is consistent with the WEF manual?
choices: The strong smell of the gas gives a dependable warning of danger
Hydrogen sulfide is harmless once the nose has adjusted to its odour
Gas leaks are a corrosion problem and carry no fire or explosion risk
Methane burns with air, and the gas can displace air and asphyxiate
checks.explanation: Methane burns with air and the gas can displace air, while the other options wrongly treat smell as a dependable warning, call hydrogen sulfide harmless once the nose adjusts, or deny any fire risk.

modules.lesson: ### Aerobic digestion in brief Aerobic digestion is a biological process that uses long-term aeration to stabilise sludge and reduce its mass by destroying volatile solids. The WEF manual says it continues until the available energy in the active cells and stored waste is low enough for the sludge to be considered stable. It may treat waste activated sludge alone, mixtures of waste activated or trickling filter sludge with primary sludge, sludge from extended aeration plants, or sludge from membrane bioreactors. The digested sludge is less likely to generate odours during disposal, and bacteriological hazards are reduced. No explosive digester gas is produced, but the gases that are produced cannot be burned for fuel the way anaerobic digester gas can. ### What the microbes are doing When the food in the sludge runs short, aerobic microbes begin to consume their own cell material to stay alive. The cells eventually break open, and the released organic matter feeds other microbes. The WEF manual calls this endogenous respiration. The end products are carbon dioxide, water and materials that do not break down further. Only about 75 to 80 percent of the cell material can be oxidised, and the rest stays as inert or non-biodegradable matter. This is why aerobic digestion reduces volatile solids and does not remove them completely. ### Oxygen, mixing and odour Oxygen is the key requirement. The WEF manual says maintaining adequate dissolved oxygen lets the biological process take place and prevents objectionable odours, and that inadequate dissolved oxygen gives incomplete digestion and, more importantly, odour problems. It gives a typical dissolved oxygen range of 0.1 to 3.0 mg/L, and daily monitoring values of about 0.4 to 0.8 mg/L are listed as nominal. For design, the manual allows about 2 pounds of oxygen per pound of volatile solids destroyed. Thick sludge is viscous. During the first stage, when oxygen demand is highest, intense mixing is essential so that oxygen transfer can occur. The manual adds that mixing needs are typically higher than the process air needs when solids concentrations are low, and that aeration and mixing devices must give enough turbulence to resuspend settled solids. ### pH and alkalinity Destroying biomass releases ammonia and alkalinity as ammonium bicarbonate. If extra oxygen turns the ammonia into nitrate, that nitrification uses up alkalinity, and the WEF manual says it is very easy to use up the alkalinity and see the pH fall to around 5, which harms the process. A study the manual reports found that high dissolved oxygen gave a low pH. If the feed has too little alkalinity, chemicals can be added, such as sodium bicarbonate to the feed or lime or sodium hydroxide to the digester. The Wisconsin monitoring table notes that carbon dioxide and nitrate, both products of aerobic digestion, tend to lower the pH. Nitrification releases acid, which uses alkalinity, and the WEF manual says closed high-purity-oxygen tanks may need neutralisation because their buffering is reduced. A different approach is to switch the aeration off for part of the day so that an anoxic period lets denitrification return alkalinity. The Wisconsin guide lists the benefits of this aerobic and anoxic operation as energy savings, nitrogen removal, pH control and phosphorus uptake (WEF: less phosphorus release). ### Temperature effects Temperature controls how fast volatile solids and pathogens are destroyed. The WEF manual says the rate of volatile solids reduction rises with temperature, and that below 10 degrees C the process is basically ineffective. In one full-scale plant the reduction was only 16 percent in a cold month even though the retention time was long. Conventional aerobic digesters operate at about 15 to 35 degrees C and are classed as mesophilic. Covers and insulation hold heat in cold climates, though too much heat can cause odours. The manual describes an SRT times temperature product, in days times degrees C, as a way to judge whether a digester has enough time at its temperature. A cold digester needs a longer SRT for the same result. ### SRT from the mass of solids Retention time can also be worked from solids rather than gallons. The WEF manual defines SRT as the total mass of biological sludge in the reactor divided by the mass of solids removed each day, averaged over time. As an example, a digester holds 90,000 gal at 2.0 percent solids, which is 90,000 x 8.34 x 0.02 = 15,012 lb of solids. If 1,500 lb of solids leave each day, the SRT is 15,012 / 1,500, about 10 days. Say which method a log entry uses, because the two can differ. ### Decanting and supernatant In a batch or draw-and-fill digester the aeration is stopped for a time, the solids settle, and the clarified supernatant is decanted and returned to the treatment process. The WEF manual describes a shut-down of one to two hours for settling in some plants, which lets more sludge be added and raises the solids concentration. The returned supernatant carries solids, BOD and nutrients back to the liquid stream, so how much is drawn off should follow the supernatant quality. ### Prethickening and retention Thickening the feed can give a longer SRT in a given tank. The WEF manual explains that a thicker feed leaves less water to heat, so the heat released by the oxidising biomass can raise the temperature and speed digestion and pathogen destruction. It reports that conventional digesters often show little temperature rise, because they are fed sludge at only about 0.5 to 1.0 percent solids. Thickened feed can be gravity thickened or mechanically thickened, and the manual links this to the thickening chapter. At the same solids feed rate, a thin feed shortens hydraulic retention time, because more volume passes through a fixed tank. ### Staged and batch operation A single tank that is completely mixed and continuously fed lets some organisms that have only been exposed to the digester for a short time leak through to the product. The WEF manual, quoting the US EPA, calls this the least effective arrangement for destroying bacteria and viruses. Two or more tanks in series, or tanks run in batches, reduce that leakage and improve pathogen destruction. Staging also means the first tank, where the demand for oxygen is highest, can be managed separately from the later ones. ### Autothermal thermophilic aerobic digestion ATAD is a variation in which the feed is prethickened to a high solids concentration and the reactors are insulated. The heat made by the microbes keeps the sludge at thermophilic temperatures without outside heat other than the aeration and mixing devices. The WEF manual gives retention times of about 5 to 6 days, while the Wisconsin guide gives 6 to 9 days, both much shorter than a conventional digester. The high temperature gives a strong reduction of pathogens and the process can produce the more stringent class of biosolids. The disadvantages are poor dewatering, objectionable odours, high capital cost, no nitrification and the need for foam control. Nitrification is inhibited, so the pH is typically 8 to 9 and ammonia leaves in the offgas and in liquid sidestreams. ### When an aerobic digester misbehaves The WEF manual's troubleshooting advice is practical. For odour from digested sludge, inadequate dissolved oxygen is the primary cause. First raise the dissolved oxygen by aerating more, then reduce the organic loading. If both fail, chemicals that oxidise the odour compounds may help, but the manual calls this expensive and temporary. For foaming, which has causes from organic overloading to filamentous bacteria, it suggests reducing organic loading, using foam-breaking water sprays sparingly so the contents are not diluted, reducing excess aeration and using defoaming chemicals. For low dissolved oxygen, check for clogged diffusers, blower trouble and organic overload. Excessive solids, around 3.5 to 4 percent, also reduce oxygen transfer. ### Lime stabilisation Lime can stabilise raw primary, waste activated and digested sludge. The WEF manual describes lime stabilisation as a high-pH condition. Its standard process example raises the sludge to a pH of 12 or more and holds it for a contact period. That describes one process, not a universal target; the applicable regulatory option and permit set any target. The high pH destroys or inhibits pathogens and the microbes that decompose sludge, so little decomposition occurs and few biological odours are produced. It can be done before dewatering or after it. It is simple to operate and has a low capital cost. The disadvantages are that the lime adds mass to dispose of, chemical use is high, and if the pH drops after treatment, microbes can regrow and odours return. Odour alone does not show adequate stabilisation. The pH has to be monitored. Lime is caustic, so protective equipment is part of working near it. ### Composting Composting is the managed biological decomposition of organic material, usually on dewatered sludge. Its objectives are to convert putrescible organics to a stable form, destroy pathogens with the heat it generates, reduce the mass of wet sludge, and make a usable product. A bulking agent is often added so that the mixture has the right solids content, a better carbon to nitrogen ratio and enough structure for air to circulate. The pile heats into the pasteurisation range, and the manual says most composting operations aim to stay aerobic because anaerobic conditions give foul odours. The costs include the bulking agent, labour for turning or forced air, land area and the potential for odour. ### Comparing the options The WEF manual's comparison table sets out the trade-offs. Composting can give a high-quality, saleable product but needs a bulking agent, labour and land. Lime stabilisation has low capital cost and is easy to operate, but it increases the volume for disposal and is chemical intensive. Digestion changes the biology of the solids and, in the anaerobic case, produces fuel gas, while aerobic digestion avoids the methane-gas hazard and costs more to aerate. The right choice depends on plant size, climate, the intended end use of the solids and what the regulator accepts. No single option is the best answer everywhere.

modules.title: Operation and records: monitoring, loading and the thickener link
objectives: Choose what to sample and record for an anaerobic or aerobic digester, take representative samples, and read trends rather than single readings.
Calculate digester loading and detention time, and explain how the output of the thickener changes the feed, retention time and recycle load of the digester.
modules.lesson: ### What to monitor in an anaerobic digester The WEF manual's monitoring table lists temperature, volatile acids, alkalinity, the VA:Alk ratio, pH, total and volatile solids, flow, gas production and gas composition. Each is listed as a daily test. Samples come from three places: the digester feed, the recirculated sludge, and the digested solids. The manual shows typical target ranges for some parameters, such as a pH of 6.8 to 7.2 and a VA:Alk ratio of 0.1 to 0.2, and asks that total solids, volatile solids and flow simply be recorded. The Wisconsin guide lists the VA:Alk ratio three times a week, with daily testing when a result is abnormal. Where sources differ, follow your own plant's procedures. ### What to monitor in an aerobic digester The WEF manual names five primary indicators for daily monitoring: temperature, pH, dissolved oxygen, odour and, where it applies, settling. Ammonia, nitrate, nitrite, phosphorus, alkalinity, SRT and the specific oxygen uptake rate, or SOUR, are secondary indicators for long-term performance and for troubleshooting. The Wisconsin guide adds that settleability matters because poor settling returns solids to the liquid treatment process. The manual says to test more often at startup and after large changes such as a new sludge source or a large change in feed solids or temperature. ### Sampling properly The WEF manual says proper sampling is critical. The sample must be representative. The pH should be measured immediately, because carbon dioxide is lost from the sample and the pH drifts. All digesters should be sampled in quick succession, sample containers should be cleaned before and after use, and a sample that cannot be analysed at once should be preserved as the test method requires. Results are then compared with earlier data. If a value looks out of range, collect and test more samples before you act on a single result unless an alarm applies,. ### Trends matter more than single numbers The manual says trend charts are an effective way to track changes in feed or operation and to predict upsets, and that the rate of change of a measurement is more significant than its absolute value. A single high or low point is not a trend, and corrective action should rest on several points showing a continued change. Early action may stop a parameter from leaving its desired range. The Wisconsin guide calls the VA:Alk ratio the first warning of problems, because volatile acids rise and alkalinity falls before the pH moves. ### A worked troubleshooting example An operator's log shows gas production falling for four days, VA:Alk climbing from about 0.15 to about 0.45, and pH still in its normal range. Temperature has held steady. The log shows the thickener was running thin for the same four days. The WEF control strategy gives the order of work. Reduce or stop the feed so the acid formers stop outrunning the methane formers. Find the cause, which here may be more volume and a swing in load, and check temperature, toxicity and mixing. Correct it, and provide pH control only until the process is back to normal. Note that the pH looks fine because the alkalinity has not yet been used up, which is exactly why the ratio is watched. ### Supernatant and digested sludge samples Feed and digesting sludge are not the only samples worth taking. The Wisconsin guide gives typical supernatant data for aerobic and anaerobic digesters, with strength in BOD, suspended solids and nitrogen and phosphorus forms that varies widely between plants, so an operator who samples supernatant learns the plant's own range. Digested sludge is checked for solids and for volume and pounds removed. A well stabilised digested sludge smells less. The Wisconsin guide gives that, and dewatering, as marks of stable sludge; dewatering alone is not proof. ### Digester loading The WEF manual says two criteria decide whether a digester can process its solids: SRT and volatile solids loading rate. At feed concentrations below about 3 percent solids, SRT usually limits capacity. At higher concentrations, volatile solids loading may be the limit. Loading rate is pounds of volatile solids fed per day divided by the active digester volume in cubic feet. The manual describes an organic overload as a loading that exceeds the daily limits by more than 10 percent, and lists erratic feeding, a change in feed composition, grit that takes up volume, and inadequate mixing among the causes. Excess organic loading is often the cause of a sour digester, so these checks come before any chemical addition. ### How thickener output reaches the digester The thickener decides the volume of sludge the digester receives for a given mass of solids. A thicker feed means longer detention time and less to heat. The WEF manual says sending sludge with the highest possible solids concentration within design conditions increases the available detention time and reduces heating needs, and that pumping dilute sludge shortens detention time. Thickening does not change the pounds of volatile solids fed unless the capture changes. It changes the gallons that carry them. A thickener that is thin one day and thick the next also swings the hydraulic load, and the manual says sudden changes in feed concentration inhibit digester performance. ### Too thick is a problem too Thicker is not always better. The WEF manual says feed at 6 or 7 percent total solids can significantly change viscosity and mixing, that pumping and mixing systems designed for lower concentrations may not support it, and that it raises volatile solids loading when more pounds of VS are fed per day,. Aerobic digesters have a related limit. The manual says oxygen transfer efficiency is reduced when suspended solids reach about 3.5 to 4 percent, so the aeration system has to be designed for the solids it will carry. A useful step is to agree a target for thickened sludge between the thickener operator and the digester operator, and write it down. ### Side streams and recycle flows Digestion produces return flows that go back to the liquid treatment train. The Wisconsin guide says sidestreams from decanting digesters or sludge storage can be high in BOD, suspended solids, ammonia, phosphorus and sulfides, or very low in temperature, and that returning them slowly and regularly lets the microorganisms acclimate. If permit limits apply to ammonia or phosphorus, the sidestream load must be known. The WEF manual adds that advanced digestion processes, with their better volatile solids reduction, can raise the soluble nutrients in dewatering recycle streams. Load is worked out as flow in million gallons per day times concentration in mg/L times 8.34, which gives pounds per day. ### Reading the troubleshooting tables The WEF manual's troubleshooting guide for anaerobic digesters is organised by symptom, probable cause, what to check and what to do, covering covers, mixing, heating, gas systems and foaming. A floating cover that tilts, for example, points to uneven weights, water or ice, or scum build-up dragging on one side. Use these tables by starting with the symptom in your log, list the likely causes, and check the simplest likely explanation first, and keep safety in view. Work inside the cover, the gas line or the tank follows your plant's written procedures, not this course. ### Foam as a signal Digester foam is fine gas bubbles trapped in a semi-liquid layer. Some foam is normal; it becomes excessive when it plugs piping or escapes. The WEF manual says the most common cause is organic overload. It lists intermittent feeding, separate feeding or poor blending of primary sludge and waste activated sludge, insufficient or intermittent mixing, and too much grease or scum in the feed as contributing factors. A rise in foam belongs in the log next to the feed schedule, because it can share causes such as organic overload with a rising VA:Alk ratio, but foam is not specific to that imbalance. ### Withdrawal and timing The WEF manual says that where withdrawal and feed are separate, solids should be withdrawn from the primary digester immediately before raw sludge is fed, to prevent short-circuiting of fresh feed out of the tank. Withdrawal at least daily keeps the microbe population and the buffering balance steady. Because digestion destroys volatile solids, the digested sludge is more dilute than the feed unless the digester is decanted. When the digested sludge is thicker than expected, check whether the digester was decanted before blaming the process. ### Keeping the right records A digester log records the feed volume, total solids and volatile solids, so that the volatile solids loading can be calculated and, with digested-sludge values, the VSR. It also holds temperature, pH, volatile acids, alkalinity and the VA:Alk ratio, gas production and gas composition, and the digested sludge volume and solids. For aerobic units it holds dissolved oxygen, pH, alkalinity, temperature, and SOUR when tested. A useful log also notes what changed, such as the sludge source, the thickener setting or a new polymer. The WEF manual says gas quantities should be measured routinely so that gas per pound of volatile solids destroyed can be compared over time. ### Safety and procedures Records and trends help you notice a problem, but they never replace procedures. Digester gas detectors and hydrogen sulfide detectors have to be calibrated regularly, and the WEF manual warns that the nose becomes numb to hydrogen sulfide, so smell is not a safe test. A confined space entry, a repair, a start-up or a shutdown follows your plant's written procedures and permits. This course describes why those controls exist and does not give the steps for any of them. ### Using this module at your plant Pick one digester log and mark the measurements the WEF manual and the Wisconsin guide ask for. Note which ones your plant takes and how often. Then trace one day of thickener data to the digester volume and estimate the detention time and the loading rate. Doing it once on paper with real numbers makes the connection between the thickener, the feed and the digester clear, and shows which gaps in the log would hide an early warning.

checks.prompt: Why should the pH of a digester sample be measured right away?
choices: The sample cools quickly, which makes the meter read too high
Carbon dioxide is lost from the sample, which shifts the pH
Volatile acids settle out of the sample within minutes
The alkalinity rises as the sample stands in the container
checks.explanation: Carbon dioxide is lost from a standing sample and shifts the pH, whereas cooling, settling acids and rising alkalinity are not the reason given.

checks.prompt: What does the WEF manual say about a single high or low data point?
choices: It is enough to justify a large change in the feed at once
It should be averaged away before anyone looks at the chart
It is not a trend, so action should rest on several points
It matters more than the long-term rate of change
checks.explanation: A single point is not a trend so action rests on several points, whereas changing the feed at once, averaging it away or ranking it above the rate of change misreads the guidance.

checks.prompt: A digester has a volume of 40,000 cu ft and is fed 6,000 lb of volatile solids per day. What is the loading rate in lb of volatile solids per day per cu ft?
choices: 0.15 lb/day/cu ft
6.67 lb/day/cu ft
0.015 lb/day/cu ft
1.5 lb/day/cu ft
checks.explanation: Loading = 6,000 / 40,000 = 0.15 lb/day/cu ft; 6.67 inverts the division and 0.015 and 1.5 misplace the decimal.

checks.prompt: How does a thicker, steady feed help an anaerobic digester?
choices: It raises the supernatant volume that returns to the plant
It lowers the mass of volatile solids fed from the same sludge
It flushes the methane formers out of the tank sooner
It gives a longer detention time and less water to heat
checks.explanation: A thicker steady feed gives longer detention and less water to heat, whereas more supernatant, less volatile solids from the same sludge or flushing out methane formers are the effects of thin feed or are untrue.

checks.prompt: A side stream is 0.08 MGD at 600 mg/L of suspended solids. Using lb per day = flow in MGD x concentration in mg/L x 8.34, how many pounds per day does it carry?
choices: 4,003 lb per day
400 lb per day
48 lb per day
40 lb per day
checks.explanation: Load = 0.08 x 600 x 8.34 = about 400 lb per day; 4,003 misplaces a decimal, 48 forgets 8.34 and 40 is a slip.

checks.prompt: Which pair of records best shows anaerobic digester performance when compared over time?
choices: Tank level and the sludge colour on each shift
Feed pump hours and the weather at the plant
Gas production and the volatile solids destroyed
Heater run time and the dates of chemical deliveries
checks.explanation: Gas production against volatile solids destroyed shows how well the biology is working, whereas level, colour, pump hours, weather and delivery dates do not.

finalAssessment.prompt: Feed to a digester is 20,000 gal per day at 2.4 percent volatile solids. Digested sludge leaves at 19,000 gal per day at 1.4 percent volatile solids. Both sludges have a specific gravity of 1.00. Using the approximate mass balance VSR = (Qfeed x VSfeed - Qdigested x VSdigested) / (Qfeed x VSfeed) x 100, what is the VSR?
choices: 44.6 percent
41.7 percent
55.4 percent
58.3 percent
finalAssessment.explanation: Flow matters because the digested sludge volume is smaller, so (20,000 x 2.4 - 19,000 x 1.4) / (20,000 x 2.4) x 100 = about 44.6 percent; 41.7 percent uses concentrations alone, and 55.4 and 58.3 percent are shares remaining, not reduction.

finalAssessment.prompt: Which part of the sludge solids does digestion mainly reduce?
choices: The fixed solids such as grit and other mineral matter
The volatile, organic solids that microbes use as food
The total water content that the sludge carries in
The dissolved salts that pass through the clarifier
finalAssessment.explanation: Digestion mainly destroys the volatile, organic solids, while grit, water and dissolved salts are not what the microbes use as food.

finalAssessment.prompt: A digester is fed 5,200 lb of volatile solids per day and achieves a VSR of 48 percent. How many pounds of volatile solids are destroyed per day?
choices: 250 lb
finalAssessment.explanation: Volatile solids destroyed = 5,200 x 0.48 = 2,496 lb per day; 2,704 lb is the amount left, 10,833 lb divides instead of multiplying and 250 lb moves the decimal.

finalAssessment.prompt: How does the Wisconsin study guide describe treated, or stable, sludge?
choices: Higher organic content, which makes it easier to store for long periods
Less odour but poorer dewatering, accepted as a trade-off
More pathogens, offset by a smaller volume to haul
Less odour, good dewatering properties and more public acceptance
finalAssessment.explanation: The guide says stable sludge has less odour, good dewatering and public acceptance, so the other options do not match the guide's description of stable sludge.

finalAssessment.prompt: A tank holds 15,000 gal of sludge at 3.0 percent solids, 65 percent of which is volatile, with a specific gravity of 1.00. Use 8.34 lb per gal. Digestion reduces the volatile solids by 40 percent. How many pounds of volatile solids remain?
choices: 976 lb
finalAssessment.explanation: Volatile solids fed = 15,000 x 8.34 x 0.03 x 0.65 = 2,439 lb and 60 percent remains, about 1,464 lb; 976 lb is the amount destroyed, 2,439 lb ignores the reduction and 3,753 lb ignores the volatile fraction.

finalAssessment.prompt: A digester destroys 3,000 lb of volatile solids per day. Assume typical gas production of 15 cu ft per lb of volatile solids destroyed. How much gas is expected per day?
choices: 200 cu ft
45,000 cu ft
4,500 cu ft
finalAssessment.explanation: Gas = 3,000 x 15 = 45,000 cu ft per day; 200 cu ft divides, 4,500 cu ft and 450,000 cu ft misplace a decimal.

finalAssessment.prompt: A sour digester has volatile acids of 300 mg/L as CaCO3 and alkalinity of 1,800 mg/L as CaCO3. Using required alkalinity = volatile acids divided by a target VA:Alk ratio of 0.1, how much alkalinity must be added, in mg/L as CaCO3?
choices: 30 mg/L
finalAssessment.explanation: Required alkalinity is 300 / 0.1 = 3,000 mg/L and 1,800 is already there, so 1,200 mg/L must be added; 3,000 forgets to subtract, 2,100 adds the 300 to the 1,800 instead of subtracting, and 30 multiplies by 0.1.

finalAssessment.prompt: VA:Alk is climbing and gas production is falling. Which first step fits the WEF control strategy?
choices: Raise the feed rate so that more methane formers can grow
Stop the mixers so that the acids settle to the floor
Heat the digester well above its normal temperature
Reduce or stop the solids feed while the cause is found
finalAssessment.explanation: The WEF strategy starts by stopping or reducing the feed, whereas raising the feed, stopping mixing or overheating make the imbalance worse.

finalAssessment.prompt: Why should digester temperature be held steady?
choices: Methane formers fail to build a stable population if it swings widely
Acid formers die quickly whenever the temperature changes even a little
Gas leaves the tank faster when it is warmer than before
Mixing stops working when the temperature moves up or down
finalAssessment.explanation: Temperature swings stop the methane formers building a stable population, while acid formers are not the sensitive group.

finalAssessment.prompt: What does pumping dilute sludge to a digester tend to do at the same daily solids load?
choices: Lengthen the detention time and lower the heating need
Shorten the detention time and add more water to heat
Raise the volatile solids reduction by adding more water
Increase the alkalinity by diluting the volatile acids
finalAssessment.explanation: Dilute feed shortens detention time and adds water to heat, so the options claiming longer detention, lower heating need, more VSR from dilution or more alkalinity reverse the effect.

finalAssessment.prompt: An aerobic digester holds 300,000 gal and is fed 15,000 gal per day at 1.0 percent solids, with no decanting. The feed is thickened to 2.5 percent solids with the same mass of solids. With no decanting in a well-mixed tank, SRT equals HRT, so using volume divided by daily feed, and with sludge density unchanged, what is the new SRT?
choices: 20 days
8 days
50 days
75 days
finalAssessment.explanation: New feed = 15,000 x 1.0 / 2.5 = 6,000 gal per day so SRT = 50 days; 20 days is the old value, 8 days divides by 2.5 and 75 days is a slip.

finalAssessment.prompt: How does an ATAD process reach thermophilic temperatures?
choices: Steam boilers heat the sludge up to the operating temperature each day
Hot water from gas engines is circulated through coils in the tank
Digester gas is burned in a heat exchanger beside the digester tank
Insulated reactors on thickened feed keep the heat the microbes make
finalAssessment.explanation: ATAD keeps its heat in insulated reactors on thickened feed, so boilers, engine heat or exchangers would be outside heat the manual says is not used.

finalAssessment.prompt: How does lime stabilisation control pathogens and odour?
choices: High pH inhibits the microbes, so little decomposition occurs
Heat from aeration destroys the volatile solids over several weeks
Methane formers use up the volatile acids in the sludge
A bulking agent supplies carbon so the microbes thrive
finalAssessment.explanation: Lime works by high pH inhibiting microbes so little decomposition occurs, not by aeration heat, methane formers or a bulking agent.

finalAssessment.prompt: Why is a bulking agent often added in composting?
choices: To lower the pH to 12 so that pathogens die
To raise the solids content and give air room to circulate
To dissolve the volatile solids before the pile is first formed
To hold the pile below pasteurisation temperatures
finalAssessment.explanation: A bulking agent raises solids content and lets air circulate, whereas a high-pH condition describes lime stabilisation, dissolving volatile solids is not its job and the pile is meant to reach pasteurisation temperatures.

finalAssessment.prompt: An aerobic digester is fed 2,500 lb of volatile solids per day and achieves a VSR of 38 percent. Allow 2 lb of oxygen per lb of volatile solids destroyed. How many pounds of oxygen are needed per day?
choices: 950 lb
finalAssessment.explanation: Volatile solids destroyed = 2,500 x 0.38 = 950 lb and oxygen = 1,900 lb per day; 950 lb forgets the factor of 2, 4,750 lb is a slip and 3,100 lb uses the volatile solids left.

finalAssessment.prompt: An anaerobic digester holds 500,000 gal and is fed 25,000 gal per day of sludge at 2.0 percent solids, with no decanting. The feed is thickened to 4.0 percent solids with the same mass of solids and sludge density unchanged. What is the new HRT in days, using HRT = volume divided by daily feed?
choices: 20 days
80 days
10 days
40 days
finalAssessment.explanation: New feed = 25,000 x 2.0 / 4.0 = 12,500 gal per day so HRT = 40 days; 20 days is the old value, 80 days would need a quarter of the original feed, and 10 days would come from doubling it.

finalAssessment.prompt: A digester has a volume of 60,000 cu ft. It is fed 20,000 gal per day of sludge at 4.0 percent solids, 75 percent of which is volatile. Use a specific gravity of 1.00 and 8.34 lb per gal. What is the volatile solids loading in lb per day per cu ft?
choices: 0.083 lb/day/cu ft
0.111 lb/day/cu ft
0.83 lb/day/cu ft
0.0083 lb/day/cu ft
finalAssessment.explanation: Volatile solids = 20,000 x 8.34 x 0.04 x 0.75 = 5,004 lb per day and 5,004 / 60,000 = about 0.083; 0.111 forgets the volatile fraction and 0.83 and 0.0083 misplace the decimal.

finalAssessment.prompt: After a thickener change, the VA:Alk ratio rises over several days while the pH stays normal. What does that suggest?
choices: Digestion is now complete, so the feed rate can safely be raised
Acids are outpacing the buffer, so an upset may be starting
The pH meter has drifted, so the rising ratio can be ignored
Alkalinity is being made faster than the acids
finalAssessment.explanation: A rising ratio with normal pH means acids are rising relative to the buffer, so it is an early warning, not completion, a meter fault or alkalinity outrunning acids.

finalAssessment.prompt: How does the Wisconsin guide say sidestreams should be returned to reduce upsets?
choices: In one large slug, so the plant sees a single short peak
Directly to the effluent channel to protect the process
Slowly and regularly, so the microorganisms can acclimate
At whatever rate empties the storage tank as soon as possible
finalAssessment.explanation: Sidestreams go back slowly and regularly so the microorganisms can acclimate, whereas a single slug shocks the plant, sending them to the effluent bypasses treatment, and draining storage as fast as possible also shocks it.

finalAssessment.prompt: An aerobic digester gives off odour. Which first step fits the WEF manual?
choices: Add an oxidising chemical straight away as a permanent fix
Cut the aeration to save energy first
Stop the mixers so the solids can settle
Check dissolved oxygen and aeration first, then raise aeration if it is low
finalAssessment.explanation: Checking dissolved oxygen first, then raising aeration if it is low, is the sound first step, whereas chemicals are expensive and temporary, cutting aeration worsens odour and stopping mixers lets solids settle.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: What does the volatile solids reduction figure tell an operator?
choices: How much water the digester has removed from the sludge
How much of the organic material fed has been destroyed
How much fixed material is left behind as grit
How many pathogens the raw sludge contained
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: VSR is the share of the organic material fed that was destroyed, not water removal, leftover grit or a pathogen count.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: A digester is fed 8,000 lb of volatile solids per day and the digested sludge carries 5,200 lb per day. Using VSR percent = (VS in minus VS out) divided by VS in, times 100, what is the VSR?
choices: 65 percent
54 percent
35 percent
15 percent
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: VSR = (8,000 - 5,200) / 8,000 x 100 = 35 percent; 65 percent is the share remaining, and 54 percent divides the reduction by the outgoing load instead of the incoming load.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: Which two processes does the Wisconsin guide list as the most common sludge treatment processes?
choices: Composting and lime stabilisation
Pasteurisation and heat drying
Thickening and mechanical dewatering
Aerobic and anaerobic digestion
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: The guide lists aerobic and anaerobic digestion as the most common processes, while composting, lime, pasteurisation and heat drying are the others and thickening and dewatering are not stabilisation.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: A digester is fed 12,000 gal per day of sludge at 5.0 percent solids, 72 percent of which is volatile. Use a specific gravity of 1.00 and 8.34 lb per gal. How many pounds of volatile solids are fed per day?
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: Volatile solids = 12,000 x 8.34 x 1.00 x 0.05 x 0.72 = about 3,603 lb per day; 5,004 lb forgets the volatile fraction and 36,029 lb misplaces a decimal.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: Why are conventional anaerobic digesters sealed?
choices: The gas has to be stored under pressure so that it can be sold
The methane formers are anaerobic, so oxygen is kept out
The acid-forming bacteria need a closed tank to reproduce
Air would raise the pH and make the volatile acids fall
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: The methane formers are anaerobic so oxygen is excluded, and the other options give reasons the manual does not, such as selling gas, helping acid formers reproduce or air raising pH.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: An anaerobic digester holds 450,000 gal and receives 25,000 gal of sludge per day, with no decanting. Using HRT in days = volume divided by daily volume removed, what is the HRT?
choices: 1.8 days
22 days
12 days
18 days
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: HRT = 450,000 / 25,000 = 18 days; 1.8 days misplaces a decimal and 22 and 12 days are slips in the division.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: Volatile acids are 450 mg/L and alkalinity is 1,500 mg/L. What is the VA:Alk ratio?
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: VA:Alk = 450 / 1,500 = 0.30; 3.33 inverts the ratio, 0.45 reuses the volatile acid figure and 0.03 misplaces a decimal.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: Why is a high-rate digester mixed?
choices: To let air in so the methane formers can breathe
To spread the feed and keep the temperature even in the tank
To settle the solids on the floor where digestion is fastest
To cool the tank so that gas production slows down
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: Mixing spreads the feed and evens the temperature, while the options about air, settling solids or cooling the tank describe things mixing is not meant to do.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: A digester makes 54,000 cu ft of gas per day while destroying 3,600 lb of volatile solids per day. How many cubic feet of gas per lb of volatile solids destroyed is that?
choices: 0.07 cu ft per lb
150 cu ft per lb
15 cu ft per lb
19 cu ft per lb
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: Gas per pound destroyed = 54,000 / 3,600 = 15 cu ft per lb; 0.07 inverts the division, 150 misplaces a decimal and 19 is a slip.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: Which use of digester gas does the WEF manual describe?
choices: A feed to the aeration basin to supply oxygen
A chemical to neutralise volatile acids in the tank
A raw feed to the primary clarifier to settle solids
Fuel for boilers that heat the digesters
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: Digester gas can fuel the boilers that heat the digesters, but it is not an oxygen feed for aeration, an acid neutraliser or raw feed to the clarifier.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: An aerobic digester runs at 16 degrees C with an SRT of 35 days. What is the SRT x temperature product in days x degrees C?
choices: 51 days x deg C
5,600 days x deg C
560 days x deg C
2.2 days x deg C
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: Product = 35 x 16 = 560 days x degrees C; 51 adds, 5,600 misplaces a decimal and 2.2 divides.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: Which statement about temperature matches the WEF manual for aerobic digesters?
choices: Cold weather speeds up the destruction of volatile solids and germs
Temperature has little influence on pathogen reduction
Above 10 degrees C the destruction of volatile solids stops
Below about 10 degrees C the process is basically ineffective
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: Below about 10 degrees C the process is basically ineffective, so cold does not speed destruction, temperature does matter to pathogens and destruction does not stop above 10 degrees C.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: How can an aerobic digester recover alkalinity without added chemicals?
choices: Switch the air off part of the day so denitrification occurs
Raise the dissolved oxygen so that more ammonia is nitrified
Feed the sludge in one large slug to boost the load
Shut the mixers down during the aeration period
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: Switching the air off part of the day lets denitrification return alkalinity, whereas raising oxygen does not recover alkalinity, since nitrification uses it up, slug feeding adds load and shutting mixers off lets solids settle.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: An aerobic digester holds 360,000 gal and is fed 18,000 gal per day at 1.5 percent solids, with no decanting. The feed is thickened to 3.0 percent solids with the same mass of solids. With no decanting in a well-mixed tank, SRT equals HRT, so using volume divided by daily feed, and with sludge density unchanged, what is the new SRT?
choices: 20 days
40 days
80 days
10 days
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: New feed = 18,000 x 1.5 / 3.0 = 9,000 gal per day so SRT = 40 days; 20 days is the old value, 80 days would need a quarter of the original feed flow, and 10 days is a slip.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: Which is an advantage of lime stabilisation in the WEF comparison table?
choices: A high-quality, saleable product for agriculture
A large cut in the sludge volume for disposal
Low capital cost and easy operation
No chemicals are needed to run the process
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: Lime stabilisation has low capital cost and easy operation, while a high-quality saleable product is listed as a composting advantage and lime actually increases sludge volume and uses chemicals.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: A digester has a volume of 75,000 cu ft and is fed 9,000 lb of volatile solids per day. What is the loading rate in lb of volatile solids per day per cu ft?
choices: 0.12 lb/day/cu ft
8.33 lb/day/cu ft
0.012 lb/day/cu ft
1.2 lb/day/cu ft
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: Loading = 9,000 / 75,000 = 0.12 lb/day/cu ft; 8.33 inverts the division and 0.012 and 1.2 misplace the decimal.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: A side stream is 0.05 MGD at 900 mg/L of suspended solids. Using lb per day = flow in MGD x concentration in mg/L x 8.34, how many pounds per day does it carry?
choices: 3,753 lb per day
375 lb per day
45 lb per day
37.5 lb per day
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: Load = 0.05 x 900 x 8.34 = about 375 lb per day; 3,753 misplaces a decimal, 45 forgets 8.34 and 37.5 is a slip.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: Why record both total solids and volatile solids of the feed?
choices: To find out how much grit the headworks removed from the flow that day
To set the polymer dose used at the thickener
To decide how much lime to add to the digester each day
To work out the volatile solids loading to the digester
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: Total and volatile solids with flow give the volatile loading; the reduction also needs digested-sludge data, whereas grit removal, polymer dose and lime dose do not come from them.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: Which feeding pattern does the Wisconsin guide favour?
choices: Thin sludge fed in large amounts once a day
Thick sludge fed in a single large batch each week
Thick sludge fed in small amounts at frequent intervals
Thin sludge fed in small amounts when gas production drops
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: The guide favours thick sludge fed in small amounts often, whereas thin feed in large doses, weekly batches or feeding when gas drops cause swings, and thin feed also shortens detention.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: A digester holds 300,000 gal and was fed 20,000 gal per day at 1.5 percent solids, with no decanting. The feed is now thickened to 3.0 percent solids with the same mass of solids and sludge density unchanged. What is the new HRT in days, using HRT = volume divided by daily feed?
choices: 30 days
15 days
60 days
7.5 days
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: New feed = 20,000 x 1.5 / 3.0 = 10,000 gal per day so HRT = 30 days; 15 days is the old value, 60 days would need a quarter of the original feed, and 7.5 days would come from doubling it.
